name: Operating Systems & Systems Security
description: Kernel and OS-level security, isolation, sandboxing, virtualization, and access control.

ccs.narrative:
Systems security at CCS has tracked the evolving boundary between kernel isolation, provenance tracking, and attack detection. The 2018 cohort established provenance as a core defensive primitive: Runtime Analysis of Whole-System Provenance (CCS 2018) demonstrated OS-level audit graphs for root-cause analysis, NodeMerge: Template Based Efficient Data Reduction For Big-Data Causality Analysis (CCS 2018) made those graphs tractable at scale, and POIROT: Aligning Attack Behavior with Kernel Audit Records for Cyber Threat Hunting (CCS 2019) operationalized threat-intelligence graphs against live audit logs. Control-flow integrity saw important advances with Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity (CCS 2018) and Where Does It Go?: Refining Indirect-Call Targets with Multi-Layer Type Analysis (CCS 2019).

Debloating emerged as a complementary attack-surface-reduction strategy, with Effective Program Debloating via Reinforcement Learning (CCS 2018) applying RL to remove unused code from production binaries. Anomaly detection moved toward continuous adaptation with Lifelong Anomaly Detection Through Unlearning (CCS 2019), which prevented false-positive accumulation by unlearning benign patterns.

From 2022, the community grappled with new kernel exploitation primitives such as DirtyCred: Escalating Privilege in Linux Kernel (CCS 2022), which bypassed modern mitigations by swapping credential objects. Provenance-based endpoint detection matured into industrial deployments, as assessed in Are we there yet? An Industrial Viewpoint on Provenance-based Endpoint Detection and Response Tools (CCS 2023).

milestones.note: Established whole-system provenance graphs as a practical basis for intrusion root-cause analysis.

milestones.note: Made provenance graph storage practical via template-based data reduction, enabling big-data causality analysis.

milestones.note: Strengthened CFI by enforcing that each indirect call site maps to a unique target, closing coarse-grained CFI gaps.

milestones.note: Applied RL to automatically remove unused code paths, reducing attack surface without breaking functionality.

milestones.note: Aligned CTI attack graphs with kernel audit logs to proactively hunt for ongoing intrusions in enterprise systems.

milestones.note: Improved call-graph precision using multi-layer type analysis, enabling tighter CFI and more accurate static analysis.

milestones.title: Lifelong Anomaly Detection Through Unlearning
milestones.note: Enabled anomaly detectors to adapt to benign behavioral drift by selectively unlearning false-positive patterns.

milestones.title: DirtyCred: Escalating Privilege in Linux Kernel
milestones.note: Introduced credential-swapping as a generic Linux privilege-escalation technique that bypasses state-of-the-art mitigations.

ndss.narrative:
Systems security at NDSS has been anchored by provenance-based threat detection and kernel-level hardening, two pillars that have grown more interconnected over time. Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things (NDSS 2018) established the importance of audit-log infrastructure; NoDoze (NDSS 2019) showed that provenance graphs could automate alert triage; and Unicorn (NDSS 2020) demonstrated that APT detection via runtime causality analysis could be both accurate and scalable—a trio of papers that together defined provenance as the dominant paradigm for endpoint threat detection at NDSS.

WATSON (NDSS 2021) abstracted high-level behaviors from fine-grained audit logs, making investigations human-comprehensible. Preventing Kernel Hacks with HAKCs (NDSS 2022) took a complementary approach, compartmentalizing kernel subsystems to contain exploits rather than merely detect them.

The 2023–2025 papers reflect diversification into embedded trust and industrial systems. MyTEE (NDSS 2023) extended trusted execution to embedded devices beyond the ARM TrustZone mainstream; Compromising Industrial Processes using Web-Based Programmable Logic Controllers (NDSS 2024) exposed a new attack surface in industrial automation; and RContainer (NDSS 2025) secured container workloads by extending ARM CCA. Across this body of work, NDSS has consistently prioritized building security primitives that are both formally grounded and deployable in real systems.

milestones.title: Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things
milestones.note: Builds a provenance-logging system for IoT homes to diagnose and audit incorrect automated device behavior.

milestones.title: NoDoze: Combatting Threat Alert Fatigue with Automated Provenance Triage
milestones.note: Reduces threat-alert fatigue by automatically triaging alerts using data-provenance graphs and anomaly scoring.

milestones.title: Unicorn: Runtime Provenance-Based Detector for Advanced Persistent Threats
milestones.note: Presents Unicorn, an anomaly-based detector using whole-system provenance graphs to detect advanced persistent threats.

milestones.title: WATSON: Abstracting Behaviors from Audit Logs via Aggregation of Contextual Semantics
milestones.note: WATSON aggregates contextual semantics from audit logs to abstract high-level behaviors for attack investigation.

milestones.title: Preventing Kernel Hacks with HAKCs
milestones.note: Enforces kernel compartmentalization using hardware memory tagging to contain exploitation across kernel components.

milestones.title: MyTEE: Own the Trusted Execution Environment on Embedded Devices
milestones.note: MyTEE builds a trusted execution environment on embedded devices lacking full TrustZone hardware extension support.

milestones.title: Compromising Industrial Processes using Web-Based Programmable Logic Controller Malware
milestones.note: Demonstrates web-based PLC malware that is more flexible, resilient, and impactful than firmware or control-logic infections.

milestones.title: RContainer: A Secure Container Architecture through Extending ARM CCA Hardware Primitives
milestones.note: Builds a secure container architecture extending ARM CCA hardware primitives to strengthen container isolation in the cloud.

sp.narrative:
Systems security at IEEE S&P covers OS kernel security, intrusion detection, and system integrity. The 2018-2019 baseline established provenance-based detection as a central paradigm: HOLMES: Real-Time APT Detection through Correlation of Suspicious Information Flows (S&P 2019) showed that graph-based correlation of system audit logs can detect sophisticated APT campaigns in real time. EnclaveDB: A Secure Database Using SGX (S&P 2018) demonstrated how SGX could protect database integrity from privileged attackers.

The 2020 wave pushed provenance analysis toward scalability and applied it to forensics. Tactical Provenance Analysis for Endpoint Detection and Response Systems (S&P 2020) showed that tagging semantics could control the provenance-graph explosion that hampers forensic analysis, while Combating Dependence Explosion in Forensic Analysis Using Alternative Tag Propagation Semantics (S&P 2020) attacked the same problem from the taint-tracking angle. Krace: Data Race Fuzzing for Kernel File Systems (S&P 2020) extended fuzzing to kernel concurrency bugs.

From 2021-2022, the provenance-graph methodology matured into production tools. SHADEWATCHER: Recommendation-guided Cyber Threat Analysis using System Audit Records (S&P 2022) applied graph neural networks to audit logs for threat detection. SoK: History is a Vast Early Warning System: Auditing the Provenance of System Intrusions (S&P 2023) synthesized a decade of provenance-based intrusion detection research.

By 2024, Kairos: Practical Intrusion Detection and Investigation using Whole-system Provenance (S&P 2024) and Flash: A Comprehensive Approach to Intrusion Detection via Provenance Graph Representation Learning (S&P 2024) demonstrated that provenance-graph methods had reached practical deployment quality, closing the loop on the research agenda HOLMES opened.

uss.narrative:
The earliest cluster here (USENIX 2018) shows OS and systems security split between two fronts: hardening the kernel attack surface and reasoning about attacks after they happen. On the offensive/defensive boundary, "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) was the watershed, demonstrating that microarchitectural side effects could shatter the most basic assumption of OS security, that the kernel address space is isolated from user space. Around it, a wave of kernel-fuzzing and exploitation work appeared: "MoonShine: Optimizing OS Fuzzer Seed Selection with Trace Distillation" (USENIX 2018) made syscall fuzzing smarter, while "FUZE: Towards Facilitating Exploit Generation for Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018) pushed toward automatically judging which kernel bugs are actually exploitable. A parallel thread tackled bloat and isolation at the software level, with "Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading" (USENIX 2018) and "Security Namespace: Making Linux Security Frameworks Available to Containers" (USENIX 2018), alongside provenance-and-forensics systems like "SAQL" and "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (both USENIX 2018) aimed at investigating long-running APT campaigns.

By 2019-2020 the field's center of gravity shifted toward fine-grained, in-process isolation, partly as a response to both Spectre/Meltdown-class leaks and the desire for least privilege without full process separation. "ERIM: Secure, Efficient In-process Isolation with Protection Keys (MPK)" (USENIX 2019) showed that Intel MPK could give cheap intra-process compartments, and "Donky" (USENIX 2020) extended that idea to RISC-V and x86. The community then immediately stress-tested the approach: "PKU Pitfalls: Attacks on PKU-based Memory Isolation Systems" (USENIX 2020) exposed real weaknesses in PKU-based schemes, a healthy attack-defense loop. In the browser, "Site Isolation: Process Separation for Web Sites within the Browser" (USENIX 2019) brought the same isolation philosophy to web origins. Meanwhile attack-surface reduction matured from static debloating ("RAZOR", USENIX 2019) into runtime, phase-aware specialization with "Temporal System Call Specialization for Attack Surface Reduction" (USENIX 2020), and kernel access-control analysis advanced through "PeX: A Permission Check Analysis Framework for Linux Kernel" (USENIX 2019) and missing-check detection.

From 2021 onward the work climbed the stack and got more automated. Fuzzing moved beyond the kernel proper to hypervisors and device interfaces, with "Nyx: Greybox Hypervisor Fuzzing using Fast Snapshots and Affine Types" (USENIX 2021) and earlier "USBFuzz" (USENIX 2020), while "SyzVegas: Beating Kernel Fuzzing Odds with Reinforcement Learning" (USENIX 2021) brought learning-based tuning to fuzzers. Isolation expanded to new runtimes and threat models, including "Swivel: Hardening WebAssembly against Spectre" (USENIX 2021) and automatic least-privilege policy generation for microservices (USENIX 2021). The latest listed work, "PROGRAPHER: An Anomaly Detection System based on Provenance Graph Embedding" (USENIX 2023), shows the forensics thread from 2018 coming full circle, now using graph embeddings and learning to detect APTs rather than just record them. Taken together, the area evolved from foundational isolation breaks and basic kernel fuzzing toward a mature ecosystem of cheap hardware-assisted compartments, automated attack-surface reduction, learning-driven testing, and provenance-based detection.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from 2018, capture three concerns that would define the area. The most consequential is "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018), which shattered the assumption that hardware memory isolation protects kernel space from user processes, kicking off a wave of microarchitectural-security research. Alongside it, the same year saw a strong push on finding kernel bugs before attackers do, with "MoonShine: Optimizing OS Fuzzer Seed Selection with Trace Distillation" (USENIX 2018) refining system-call fuzzing, and "FUZE: Towards Facilitating Exploit Generation for Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018) automating exploitability assessment. A parallel thread tackled isolation and attack-surface reduction: "Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading" (USENIX 2018) and "Effective Program Debloating via Reinforcement Learning" (CCS 2018) cut away unused code, while "Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity" (CCS 2018) tightened CFI defenses.

The second major theme, which quickly grew to dominate this set by citation count, is provenance- and audit-log-based attack detection. Even in 2018, "Towards a Timely Causality Analysis for Enterprise Security" (NDSS 2018) and "SAQL: A Stream-based Query System for Real-Time Abnormal System Behavior Detection" (USENIX 2018) framed intrusion investigation as a problem over system-event graphs, while "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (USENIX 2018) and "NodeMerge: Template Based Efficient Data Reduction" (CCS 2018) attacked the resulting data-volume problem. In 2019 this matured into real-time APT detection with "HOLMES: Real-Time APT Detection through Correlation of Suspicious Information Flows" (S&P 2019), and confronted the operational pain of false positives in "NoDoze: Combatting Threat Alert Fatigue with Automated Provenance Triage" (NDSS 2019), with "POIROT" (CCS 2019) reframing detection as threat hunting by aligning attack behavior to kernel audit records.

Across 2019-2020 the isolation and fuzzing threads kept advancing in parallel. "ERIM: Secure, Efficient In-process Isolation with Protection Keys (MPK)" (USENIX 2019) showed lightweight intra-process isolation using new hardware primitives, while "SANCTUARY" (NDSS 2019) and the cautionary "SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems" (S&P 2020) charted both the promise and the fragility of ARM TrustZone enclaves. Kernel bug-finding sharpened around the hard case of concurrency, with "Razzer: Finding Kernel Race Bugs through Fuzzing" (S&P 2019), "HFL: Hybrid Fuzzing on the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2020), and "Krace: Data Race Fuzzing for Kernel File Systems" (S&P 2020). On detection, "Unicorn: Runtime Provenance-Based Detector for Advanced Persistent Threats" (NDSS 2020) and "Tactical Provenance Analysis for Endpoint Detection and Response Systems" (S&P 2020) pushed graph-based methods toward practical EDR deployment.

The most recent papers show the field consolidating around learning over provenance graphs. "SHADEWATCHER: Recommendation-guided Cyber Threat Analysis" (S&P 2022) borrowed recommendation-system techniques, "PROGRAPHER: An Anomaly Detection System based on Provenance Graph Embedding" (USENIX 2023) leaned on graph embeddings, and "Kairos: Practical Intrusion Detection and Investigation using Whole-system Provenance" (S&P 2024) aimed at practical, whole-system detection and investigation together. Taken as a whole, the area moved from foundational shocks to isolation guarantees (Meltdown, ERIM, TrustZone), through systematic kernel bug discovery (MoonShine, Razzer, HFL, Krace), and converged on increasingly automated, machine-learning-driven analysis of system audit data as the dominant frontier for detecting stealthy, long-running intrusions.
